method: POST /api/chat against the running Docker app; existing and newly collected live evidence
question: Compare the publishers' reported City and West End prime rents for Q2 2026. Where do the sources disagree, and what can we conclude?
vector_backend: Qdrant service used by the running app

response.answer:
Partial brief: individually verified claims

Key Metrics
1. Fact: Savills' Q2 2026 City prime rent of £116.73 per sq ft sits below its own Q1 2026 figure of £130.80 per sq ft; both belong to Savills' average prime rent series, so this is a period movement within one series rather than a publisher disagreement. [1] [2]
2. Interpretation: The apparent Q1-to-Q2 fall in Savills' City series may reflect that the Q1 average was lifted by trophy-building transactions, including a record £160 per sq ft top rent, so an average achieved prime rent can be deal-mix sensitive rather than a quoting level. [2] [1]
3. Fact: Savills notes 11 City transactions above £100 per sq ft year-to-date in Q2 2026, almost matching the total for the whole of 2025, and the highest Q2 West End rent achieved was £182.50 per sq ft at Devonshire House, Mayfair. [1]

Emerging Signals
1. Interpretation: Both retrievable Q2 2026 sources point to demand polarisation toward premium space supporting top-end rents, consistent with prime-versus-secondary bifurcation, though prime rent levels alone do not establish rental growth outperformance. [1] [5]

Watchlist
1. Interpretation: To settle whether publishers genuinely disagree on Q2 2026 City and West End prime rents, the Knight Frank Q2 2026 rent section needs to be obtained, as its rent tables sit beyond the indexed portion of the report. [5]

Disagreements
1. Interpretation: Savills' Q2 2026 West End average prime rent of £175.10 per sq ft and Knight Frank's most recent retrievable West End Core headline rent of £185.00 per sq ft (Q4 2025) should not be read as conflicting: they come from different publishers, definitions (average achieved prime vs core headline quoting rent) and observation periods. [1] [3]
2. Interpretation: On the available evidence there is no verifiable publisher disagreement on Q2 2026 prime rents: only Savills provides Q2 2026 figures, and its passages are internally consistent across duplicate report versions (City £116.73, West End £175.10). [1] [4]

Evidence gaps
Knight Frank's Q2 2026 report was retrieved, but the indexed text does not include its prime rent section or headline rent table, so KF's Q2 2026 City Core and West End Core prime rents could not be verified
No Q2 2026 prime rent figures from any publisher other than Savills were retrievable, so a true multi-publisher comparison is not possible
Publisher methodologies differ (average achieved prime rents vs headline/core quoting rents), limiting like-for-like comparability even where figures exist across periods
No verdict-style hypothesis was tested; this is a factual comparison constrained by coverage
Some claims failed citation checks and were omitted. The remaining claims do not establish an overall conclusion.

On the available evidence there is no verifiable publisher disagreement on Q2 2026 prime rents: only Savills provides Q2 2026 figures, and its passages are internally consistent across duplicate report versions (City £116.73, West End £175.10).

Savills notes 11 City transactions above £100 per sq ft year-to-date in Q2 2026, almost matching the total for the whole of 2025, and the highest Q2 West End rent achieved was £182.50 per sq ft at Devonshire House, Mayfair.

Both retrievable Q2 2026 sources point to demand polarisation toward premium space supporting top-end rents, consistent with prime-versus-secondary bifurcation, though prime rent levels alone do not establish rental growth outperformance.
